evidence.label: The sharp logarithmic exponent of r(5,t)
Sharp logarithmic exponents for fixed off-diagonal Ramsey numbers
Lean scope doc
evidence.note: 2 papers. The scope doc links 2 Comparator challenges for main results.

headline: For every fixed s ≥ 5, the Ramsey number r(s,t) now has its exact power of log t, up to a vanishing error.
scope: The result covers every fixed clique size s of at least 5, as t grows. It fixes the power of log t, not the constant factor in front.
plain: The Ramsey number r(s,t) is the fewest people at a party that guarantees s mutual friends or t mutual strangers. For fixed s, an upper bound of order t^(s−1)/(log t)^(s−2) has stood since 1980. Lower bounds matched the power of t only recently, and still lost a larger power of log t. These two papers prove the upper bound's power of log t is right, up to an error that shrinks as t grows.
doesNot: This does not cover s = 4, and it does not find the constant factor in front of t^(s−1)/(log t)^(s−2).
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Paul Erdős and George Szekeres, the first general upper bound
scorecard.significanceWhy: It closes the logarithmic gap between lower and upper bounds for a central family of Ramsey numbers.

explanation:
Six people meet at a party. Any two are either friends or strangers. However the friendships fall, some three are all friends, or some three are all strangers. With five people this can fail. Seat them in a ring, make each person friends with the two beside them, and no such trio appears. So the Ramsey number r(3,3) is 6.

In general, r(s,t) is the fewest people that forces s mutual friends or t mutual strangers. In graph terms, a clique is a set of vertices all linked to each other. An independent set has no links at all. Ramsey's theorem from 1930 says these numbers are always finite[1]. This entry is about the off-diagonal case: s stays fixed while t grows large.

Upper bounds came first. Erdős and Szekeres gave one in 1935, which grows like t^(s−1). In 1980 Ajtai, Komlós and Szemerédi divided that by (log t)^(s−2)[2]. That upper bound is where the target power s − 2 comes from[3]. For s = 3, Kim showed in 1995 that this upper bound is right up to a constant[4].

For larger s, lower bounds lagged far behind. For s = 5, random constructions could not even reach the right power of t[5]. Finite geometry changed this. In 2026 Bradač built graphs that match the power t^(s−1) for every fixed s[6]. But his bound divides by (log t)^(2s−4), not (log t)^(s−2). That leftover is the gap these papers close[7].

Put numbers on that gap for s = 5. The upper bound is about t⁴/(log t)³ and Bradač's lower bound is about t⁴/(log t)⁶. Take t equal to one million, so log t is about 13.8. Then (log t)³ is about 2,637 and (log t)⁶ is about 6.95 million. The two bounds differ by a factor of about 2,637.

The first paper proves that for s = 5 the true power of log t is 3[8]. For every small ε above zero, r(5,t) is at least t⁴/(log t)^(3+ε) once t is large enough. It is at most a constant times t⁴/(log t)³. The second paper proves the same pattern for every fixed s of at least 6, with power s − 2[9]. The constant factor in front stays open[10].

The papers build graphs from geometry over a finite field. Each vertex gets a random point and a random hyperplane through it. A hyperplane is a flat slice one dimension lower than the space. Links depend on which points lie on which hyperplanes. Linear algebra then rules out the forbidden clique[11]. The hard part is the other side: showing no large independent set exists. Picking out one long independent sequence can skew its statistics badly[12]. The first paper's main new tool describes pairs of point sets and hyperplane sets that meet far less often than expected[13]. The second paper gives all its own arguments, including new steps for higher dimensions[14].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked formal versions of both theorems, with their lower and upper bounds. No specialist review of either paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major. Lean checks formal versions of both theorems. The constant factor stays open, s = 4 is not covered, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: The smallest number of vertices that forces either s vertices all linked to each other or t vertices with no links among them.
A set of vertices in a graph that are all linked to each other.
A set of vertices in a graph with no links among them.
The case where s stays fixed while t grows, instead of both growing together.
The power of log t in a formula like t⁴/(log t)³; here it is 3.
An error term that shrinks toward zero as t grows.
